The repetition of “must” (すべく) underscores an inner necessity that overrides the ambiguity of “near or far.”

By refusing to resolve the spatial uncertainty, the haiku converts an external problem of perception into an internal drama of will. The plum blossoms, conventional symbols of fleeting beauty and renewal, here become the occasion for a decisive act rather than quiet contemplation. This tension is heightened by the poem’s extreme brevity: five-seven-five syllables leave no room for explanation, so the force of determination must be felt in the stark grammar itself. The result is a haiku that celebrates resolve without promising arrival, suggesting that the moral weight of a journey lies in the decision to set out rather than in the certainty of its end.

The result is a poem whose surface brightness is undercut by an undercurrent of desperation—the speaker must keep naming the month lest the heart, once more, refuse to open.

This tension between declared fortune and depicted obscurity produces a restrained but pointed critique of seasonal optimism; renewal is acknowledged only as a rumor glimpsed through conditions that continue to deny it.
